parts.title: Looking for a “Money-Making Personality”? The Main Character Was Your Past Self
parts.part1:
“If you take things more seriously, will you earn more?”
“Or do you start taking things more seriously after you earn more?”

When you hear about studies on income and personality, you may expect to learn the “secret of people who earn a lot.” But this time, the people in the story are not rich people. They are “your past self” and “your later self.”

The research brought together 11 large studies. They looked at people who had jobs and shared information about their personality and work income. The number of people was not the same in every study. The researchers used data from up to 134,515 people. Each study measured the same people’s income and personality at least three times.

The important thing was how the researchers compared people. They looked separately at differences between people that usually stay the same. They also looked at changes inside each person.
parts.part2:
Not, “What’s different between me and that person who earns a lot?”
But, “How are my past self and my later self different?”

In a way, the researchers stopped comparing people with others. Instead, they followed each person over time. It is like putting down binoculars you use to look at your neighbor’s greener grass. Then you turn the pages of your own records.

Then came “diligence.” This means taking things seriously and working hard. When a person’s income went up, their diligence tended to rise later too. This link was small. The link also went the other way. When diligence rose, income tended to rise later. That link was small too.

It was not a link in only one direction. It went both ways. But this is important, so let me say it clearly: the links were “small.”

“So, earning more makes me more serious!”
Wait before you jump to that conclusion.
parts.part3:
This study cannot show that higher income changed a person’s personality. It also cannot show that their personality made their income rise. Something else may have played a part in both. Even when researchers follow the same people and compare them carefully, this alone cannot show what caused what.

In other words, this is not a how-to guide for a “personality that earns more.” This study can give you a reason to open again a book you were about to close. You may have thought, “This is just the kind of person I am.”

Instead of ending with, “That person is the kind who earns a lot,” you can look back and ask, “How have I changed?” You may plan to flip through a book about successful people. Then you may realize you are reading the next part of your own story. That is what makes this study interesting.
parts.in_one_line: Over time, income changes and later diligence changes had small links both ways. The study cannot show what caused what, but it can make us ask how we changed.

parts.title: Looking for a “Money-Making Personality”? The Main Character Turned Out to Be Your Former Self
parts.part1:
“If you become more serious, will you earn more?”
“Or do you become more serious once you start earning more?”

When you hear about research on income and personality, you might expect to learn the “secret of high earners.” But this time, the people in the spotlight are not some rich people. They are “your former self” and “your later self.”

The research brought together 11 large studies. They looked at people who were working and had reported on their personality and income from work. The number of people varied by analysis, but the researchers used data from as many as 134,515 people. In every study, the same people’s income and personality were measured at least three times.

The key was how the researchers compared people. They analyzed separately the differences between people that tend not to change and changes that happen within each person.
parts.part2:
Not, “What’s different between me and that person who earns a lot?”
But, “How are my former self and my later self different?”

In a way, the researchers shifted from comparing yourself with others to keeping track of yourself over time. It’s like putting down your binoculars for looking at your neighbor’s greener grass and turning the pages of your own records.

Then came “diligence.” Think of it as a personality that takes things seriously and works hard. There was a small positive link between changes in a person’s income and later changes in their diligence. In the other direction, there was also a small positive link between changes in diligence and later changes in income.

It wasn’t a one-way link, but a two-way one. But this is important, so let me stress it: the links were “small.”

“So, earning more turns me into a more serious person!”
Hold on before jumping to that conclusion.
parts.part3:
This study cannot tell us that income changed a person’s personality, or that their personality increased their income. Something else may have played a part in both. Even if researchers follow the same people and take care in how they compare them, that alone cannot prove what caused what.

In other words, this is not a how-to guide to a “personality that earns more.” It is a study that can give you a reason to reopen the book you were about to close, thinking, “This is just the kind of person I am.”

Rather than ending with “That person is the type who earns a lot,” you can look back and ask, “How have I changed?” You may plan to flip through a book about successful people, then realize you’re reading the sequel to your own story. That is what makes this study interesting.
parts.in_one_line: Tracking people over time, researchers found small links in both directions between changes in income and later changes in diligence. The study cannot show what caused what, but it offers a reason to ask how we ourselves have changed.
